5eX6j2j6gfaXEryl54oIKZ.title: If You're Ready (Come Go With Me)

s.t: Mavis Staples almost didn’t want to record it, because she thought it sounded just like the Staple Singers’ earlier hit ‘I’ll Take You There’.
s.src: Cross Rhythms: The Staple Singers chronicle
s.q: I almost didn't want to do that song because I said, 'It sounds just like "I'll Take You There".'

s.t: For a Muscle Shoals session with The Staple Singers, Stax songwriter Carl Hampton shipped his piano to his hotel to pair as many songs as possible.
s.src: Stax Songwriter Series: Carl Hampton and Homer Banks
s.q: Hampton shipped his piano to his hotel to ensure that he and his songwriting partners would pair as many songs as possible

s.t: Homer Banks, who wrote the Staple Singers' ‘If You're Ready (Come Go with Me)’, also wrote ‘A Lot of Love’, whose music formed the basis of the Spencer Davis Group's ‘Gimme Some Lovin'’.
s.q: Banks had greater success with the Staple Singers; "A Lot of Love" formed the musical basis of the Spencer Davis Group hit single "Gimme Some Lovin'"

s.t: Raymond Jackson, who co-wrote it with Homer Banks and Carl Hampton, died in November 1972 at the age of 31.
s.q: Raymond Earl Jackson (September 11, 1941 – November 10, 1972) ... "If You're Ready (Come Go With Me)", both co-written with Banks and Carl Hampton ... in November 1972, at the age of 31.

f.t: Bob Dylan said their gospel record ‘Uncloudy Day’ was ‘the most mysterious thing I’d ever heard’, and that Mavis Staples’s singing ‘just knocked me out’.
f.q: It was the most mysterious thing I'd ever heard ... I'd think about them even at my school desk ... Her singing just knocked me out

f.t: When Al Bell first brought them to the Swampers' Alabama studio in 1970, the family was surprised to discover that the band behind the Muscle Shoals soul hits was white.
f.src: PopMatters - How the Staple Singers Became the Soul of Protest Music
f.q: When Bell first brought the Staples to the Swampers’ Alabama studio in 1970, the family was surprised to discover that the band behind those songs was white.

f.t: At the age of eight, Mavis Staples was already a standout; she later recalled people coming up crying and putting money in her hand without her understanding why.
f.src: Los Angeles Review of Books - Freedom at the End of a Gospel Song
f.q: People would come up crying and put money in my hand, and I didn't understand.

f.t: Roebuck ‘Pops’ Staples, their founder, paid fifty cents a week towards a Stella guitar at 14, then put it down for a dozen years while working in a slaughterhouse.
f.src: Forgotten Heroes: Pops Staples – Premier Guitar
f.q: By age 14 Staples was paying fifty cents a week towards a Stella he saw hanging in a store window. ... Staples put the guitar down for a dozen years while working in a slaughterhouse

f.t: Steve Cropper said of their founder Roebuck ‘Pops’ Staples: ‘Everybody wanted to copy that tremolo sound, because he was one of the first guys to do it.’
f.src: Steve Cropper discusses Pops Staples' underrated contributions
f.q: Everybody wanted to copy that tremolo sound, because he was one of the first guys to do it.

f.t: Their founder Roebuck ‘Pops’ Staples moved to Will Dockery's plantation near Drew, Mississippi, around 1923, where Charley Patton and Howlin' Wolf inspired him to take up guitar.
f.q: was inspired to take up guitar by local blues artists Charley Patton, Howlin’ Wolf, Dick Bankston, and Jim Holloway

f.t: Their 1972 hit ‘I’ll Take You There’ opens with a groove from ‘The Liquidator’, a 1969 reggae instrumental by Harry J Allstars.
f.q: The song's intro came from "The Liquidator," a 1969 reggae instrumental from Harry J Allstars.
